solution: Executives get consecutive blocks from the front, so the answer is the maximum number of parts in a left-to-right split of the array whose block sums are non-decreasing. Run a prefix DP that stores, for every prefix, the Pareto-best pair (largest number of blocks, and the smallest last-block sum attaining it): dp[i] takes the best j < i with pre[i]-pre[j] >= last[j], breaking ties toward the largest j so the new last block is as small as possible. More blocks never hurt and a smaller last block never hurts, so one pair per prefix suffices; the fuzz confirms this against exhaustive splits. O(N^2) time with N <= 3000, O(N) space.
statement_summary: N briefcases, each holding some bananas, are handed out in order to executives ranked by evilness: each executive receives a positive number of the lowest-numbered briefcases still available. A more evil executive must end up with at least as many bananas as every less evil one. With N up to three thousand, the task is to maximise how many executives can be rewarded.
notes: dp-on-dag is not applicable: the only DAG here is the DP's own prefix-to-prefix state graph, not a graph the problem hands you. The interesting part is that keeping a single Pareto pair per prefix is sound; the verify script checks that against all 2^(n-1) splits. Statement contains no sentence addressed to the annotator.
